title: 3-Read Friday #60: CPD Culture, Cognitive Architecture, and Worksheet Design
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 60 pairs a caution about CPD implementation with two pieces on the theory and practice of teaching maths. Barton opens with Claire Stoneman's warning against letting strategies become empty box-ticking exercises, quoting her line about 'fiddling while Rome burns' as his favourite from the piece. He then recommends Paul Kirschner's essay on whether all students learn the same way, praising the digestive-system analogy as the best explanation he's read of how shared cognitive architecture and individual differentiation can both be true at once. His third pick is Dylan Kane's walkthrough of a worksheet on simplifying algebraic expressions, which Barton flags as being 'for the maths geeks' interested in the reasoning behind resource design decisions.
points: Barton's choice to quote Stoneman's 'fiddling while Rome burns' line directly, rather than paraphrasing it, signals that the exact phrasing -- not just the underlying point about surface-level strategy adoption -- is what struck him.
He explicitly calls Kirschner's piece 'the best post I have read' on the sameness/difference question in learning, an unusually strong superlative compared to his typical measured recommendations.
His framing of the Kane worksheet pick around 'his decisions when creating it' shows Barton valuing the meta-level reasoning behind a resource as much as the resource itself.

The issue's spread -- CPD implementation, cognitive theory, and granular resource design -- again shows Barton's habitual range across school-leadership, research, and classroom-craft layers within a single roundup.
quotes: Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.
This is an important post from Claire, urging leaders to be cautious when suggesting (or requesting!) colleagues implement new strategies and ideas.
Unless the strategies and tools translate into teacher thought and – crucially – _pupil thought_ (because that’s why we’re doing what we’re doing, right?), we’re just fiddling while Rome burns”.
This is the best post I have read to address the question of whether all students learn the same way and, if so, what the implications are for teaching.
One for the maths geeks! Here, Dylan shares a worksheet on simplifying algebraic expressions, talking through his decisions when creating it.
